text:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Thank you for waiting, Doctor. Let us take the evening in order. You dined here?

DR VAUTHIER: I did, Inspector. I have dined at this table for thirty years, and Aurèle keeps the custom of the year's end as carefully as he keeps his escapements.

MATTHEY: What happened at dinner, when the temple bell struck nine?

DR VAUTHIER: Aurèle asked us all to show him our watches. He does it every year. It is his joke and his tyranny. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. I showed him, and he grunted, which from Aurèle is a considerable concession.

MATTHEY: And afterwards?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame and I sat down to piquet in the salon. Odile plays a hard game, Inspector, and a cold one. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch.

MATTHEY: What happened then?

DR VAUTHIER: I wanted my cigar case, which was in my coat in the hall, so I went out to fetch it. Odile began to play the piano as I went out. She plays Chopin, and she plays him better than anyone in the canton.

MATTHEY: Did she stop?

DR VAUTHIER: She stopped when I came back.

MATTHEY: And then?

DR VAUTHIER: I sat down again, and the hall clock struck eleven a moment after I did. The old Morbier. It strikes by its own face, and one learns to listen to it as one listens to a difficult patient.

MATTHEY: You examined Aurèle's body.

DR VAUTHIER: I did, when I was called to him. A blow to the back of the head. One heavy stroke, from behind. I would say he knew very little of it, and that death would have been very quick. That is a physician's opinion and I will stand by it. What I cannot give you is an hour of death. Anyone who offers you one from a body alone is selling you a watch that does not run.

MATTHEY: You attended Jules Monnier in his last illness.

DR VAUTHIER: In 1889. A dreadful business. Jules was Aurèle's younger brother, and he bore his illness with a bad grace and a good deal of brandy. I sat with him at the end. Félix was a young man then, and I think he has never quite forgiven the illness for taking his father.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear.

DR VAUTHIER: I have been clear for thirty years, Inspector. It is the only virtue my patients have ever allowed me. Tempus edax rerum, as the Romans said. Time is a hungry thing, and this year it has been hungrier than most. Would you care for a cigar?
